stories.headline: NVIDIA CRUSHES Q2, GUIDES 70% REVENUE GROWTH AS SHARES RISE AFTER HOURS
stories.body: Nvidia posted fiscal Q2 revenue of $96.22 billion, up 106% year-over-year and above the $92.17 billion Wall Street expected, with adjusted EPS of $2.22 versus $2.08 estimated. CEO Jensen Huang said AI demand is accelerating, and the company guided to $108 billion in current-quarter sales against a $104.2 billion consensus; shares rose in after-hours trading, snapping a seven-session losing streak heading into the print.
stories.explain: Nvidia's report is the single biggest read-through for the AI capex cycle, since hyperscaler chip spending is the metric markets use to judge whether trillions in projected AI infrastructure investment is actually materializing. The stock's reaction hinges more on the $108 billion guide clearing the $104.2 billion consensus than on the trailing quarter's beat, because forward guidance reprices the entire future earnings stream rather than just the quarter that already happened, which is what actually moves a stock priced for this much growth.

stories.headline: CORE INFLATION HOLDS AT 3.3% AS MARKETS BRACE FOR WARSH'S FIRST JACKSON HOLE SPEECH
stories.body: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge showed core PCE up 3.3% year-over-year in July, its fourth straight month at that level, while headline PCE held at 3.7% — both released Wednesday morning ahead of the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, which opens Thursday. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first keynote as chair Friday at 10 a.m. ET, addressing this year's theme of financial innovation in payments and policy.
stories.explain: A Jackson Hole speech moves markets less for what it says about the next meeting than for the reaction function it reveals: how the Fed will weigh a labor market showing cracks against inflation stuck three points above target. Core PCE holding flat for a fourth straight month gives Warsh room to frame inflation as contained without declaring victory, which is why Treasury yields barely moved on today's data — traders are waiting for Friday's tone, not today's number, to reset the path to the Sept. 16 decision.

stories.headline: OIL SLIPS AS IRAN SANCTIONS FALL SHORT OF EXPECTATIONS; GOLD WHIPSAWS NEAR $4,600
stories.body: WTI crude fell roughly 1.9% to $81 a barrel after Washington's latest sanctions push on Iran proved less aggressive than markets had priced in, easing supply-disruption fears built up over months of regional tension. Gold swung between roughly $4,715 and $4,594 an ounce intraday, ending near the lower end of that range as the dollar firmed, though it remains up more than 12% over the past month.
stories.explain: Oil's move is a probability repricing, not a supply change: traders had built a premium into the barrel for the odds of tighter enforcement disrupting Iranian exports, and that premium can unwind in a session once the actual measures come in softer than feared. Gold's wide intraday swing reflects two competing forces pulling at once — a firmer dollar and steady yields pressuring it lower, against persistent U.S. debt-load concerns that have driven its 35% year-over-year run, which is why the metal round-tripped several percentage points without a clear directional resolution today.

stories.headline: TRUMP SETS 50% TARIFFS ON CANADIAN AUTOS AND STEEL FOR 2027 AFTER TALKS COLLAPSE
stories.body: President Trump announced the U.S. will raise tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts, and steel to 50% effective Jan. 1, 2027, doubling the current 25% duty on Canadian auto imports, after trade talks between the two countries broke down. Canadian steel already faces a 50% levy; the White House says U.S.-built vehicles are exempt.
stories.explain: Tariffs are collected from the U.S. importer of record, so the immediate mechanism is higher input costs passed to American automakers and buyers unless thin-margin Canadian exporters absorb the hit, which they have little room to do. Markets are treating the four-month runway to the January effective date as a negotiating window rather than a certainty, which is part of why the news moved industrial and auto names more than the broad index today.

stories.headline: U.S. NATIONAL DEBT TOPS $40 TRILLION AS TREASURY LEANS ON DEBT BUYBACKS
stories.body: Total U.S. government debt crossed $40.05 trillion this week, a milestone reached as the Treasury continues an expanded debt buyback program aimed at smoothing bond-market liquidity and managing the government's rising interest bill. The dollar index still traded near a three-month low despite today's modest 0.2% gain, with fiscal concerns cited as a persistent drag.
stories.explain: Debt buybacks let Treasury retire older, less-liquid bonds and reissue new ones, which can lower borrowing costs at the margin, but the practice also signals how much active balance-sheet management is now required just to keep the Treasury market functioning smoothly at this debt level. The $40 trillion figure matters to markets less as a single alarming number and more as a trend line: it shapes how much fiscal risk gets priced into the dollar and long-end yields, which is the same debt-load concern currently keeping gold's multi-month rally intact.

stories.headline: RJ LUIS ELIGIBILITY FIGHT DEEPENS AS COURTS AND CONFERENCES COLLIDE OVER PRO-CONTRACT RULE
stories.body: Former G-Leaguer RJ Luis remains in eligibility limbo at LSU: a Louisiana state court previously ruled him eligible to play under Will Wade, but a new Big Ten push to extend the football pro-contract ban into basketball would render him ineligible under conference bylaws if adopted league-wide. Elsewhere, Yale transfer Nick Townsend committed to Stanford and St. John's landed a commitment from Keyshawn Hall as rosters keep shifting three months from tip-off.

stories.headline: TRAIL BLAZERS' SHAEDON SHARPE OUT ~6 MONTHS WITH TORN MENISCUS AS FREE AGENCY GRINDS ON
stories.body: Portland guard Shaedon Sharpe is expected to miss roughly six months after tearing his meniscus, a significant blow to the Blazers' backcourt heading into the season. Elsewhere, Klay Thompson signed a two-year, $11.48 million deal with Miami, Brandon Williams joined Golden State on a one-year deal, and Detroit's Jalen Duren remains unsigned in a contract standoff that has made him a trade candidate, reportedly drawing interest from Toronto.

stories.headline: 2026 SEASON OPENS SEPT. 9 WITH PATRIOTS-SEAHAWKS SUPER BOWL 60 REMATCH
stories.body: The NFL's regular season kicks off Wednesday, Sept. 9, with New England traveling to face Seattle in a rematch of Super Bowl 60, airing at 7 p.m. ET on NBC and Peacock. Elsewhere, Patrick Mahomes' recovery from a torn ACL remains the Chiefs' central storyline, Atlanta's Michael Penix Jr. sat out the preseason finale with the Falcons' QB battle still unresolved, and Giants receiver Calvin Austin is out for the season with a torn ACL.

stories.headline: BIG TEN, SEC BAN PLAYERS WITH PRO CONTRACTS FROM RETURNING, THREATEN COACH SUSPENSIONS
stories.body: The Big Ten and SEC both adopted bylaws barring any player who signed a professional contract, appeared on a pro roster, or declared for a draft without withdrawing from competing at a member school; violating schools face fines and a head coach suspension for half the season. The move comes three days before the season opens Saturday, amid a wave of state-court rulings granting eligibility outside the NCAA's own process.

sports.detail: Season opens Sept. 6 vs. Washington State, 4 p.m. ET on NBC at Husky Stadium, which rolls out new Evolv security screening and expanded gameday traditions in 2026. Third-year coach Jedd Fisch's Huskies host seven games this season, including four Big Ten matchups and the Apple Cup.

Finished 16-17 (7-13 Big Ten) last season, missing the NCAA Tournament. Lost top scorer Hannes Steinbach (drafted 14th by Charlotte) and No. 2 scorer Zoom Diallo (transferred to Kentucky); Wesley Yates III (13 ppg) returns to lead a retooled roster into the 2026 Big Ten slate.

Fell to Tennessee to go 0-2 in the preseason, with safety Bud Clark and lineman Mason Richman landing on injured reserve from that game. Face the Chiefs at Arrowhead Friday, Aug. 28 at 5 p.m. PT in the preseason finale; Devon Witherspoon signed a four-year extension, and the season opens Sept. 9 at home vs. New England in a Super Bowl 60 rematch.

Coming off the East's best regular-season record, Detroit opens 2026-27 at home vs. Boston before a three-game trip to Miami, Philadelphia, and New York. The offseason's biggest loose end is center Jalen Duren, unsigned in a contract dispute that has stirred trade buzz with Toronto.

Beat the Phillies 4-1 today at T-Mobile Park: Cal Raleigh homered in four straight at-bats to tie a team record, and George Kirby held Philadelphia to one run into the eighth inning. Seattle remains in the thick of the AL wild-card race down the stretch; the two teams continue their series Thursday.

deepDive.title: Why the Guidance Beat the Headline: Reading Nvidia's Forward Numbers
content: The S&P 500 barely moved today, down 0.02%, even with a steady core PCE reading and a Canadian tariff escalation in the mix — because the session's real catalyst was arriving after the closing bell. Nvidia's fiscal Q2 revenue of $96.22 billion beat consensus by about $4 billion, a headline number that would normally move a stock. But the figure that actually mattered more was the $108 billion guide for the current quarter, comfortably above the $104.2 billion Wall Street had modeled. Understanding why a forward number outweighs a trailing beat is the key to reading how markets priced Nvidia tonight, and why guidance-driven reactions are a distinct phenomenon from ordinary earnings surprises.

Equity prices are forward-discounting mechanisms: a stock's value reflects the present value of all its future cash flows, not the quarter that just ended. When Nvidia beats trailing revenue by $4 billion, analysts revise one already-known data point. When it guides $3.8 billion above consensus for the quarter ahead, analysts must revise their entire model — not just next quarter, but the growth trajectory implied for every quarter after it, since sell-side models chain estimates together using assumed sequential growth rates. A single guidance number therefore cascades through several future quarters of estimates at once, which is why it carries a disproportionate multiplier on the stock's valuation relative to a same-sized trailing beat.

This is also why high-multiple growth stocks can fall on a headline beat: when a company is priced for perfection, merely meeting sky-high expectations without also raising the forward bar reads as disappointing, because the stock's valuation had already assumed acceleration. Nvidia itself illustrates the pattern — it has beaten Wall Street's consensus in 22 of its last 24 quarters, yet its stock reaction has varied enormously quarter to quarter depending on whether the guide matched, missed, or exceeded the market's implicit assumption of continued acceleration, not the beat itself.

The mechanism reaches beyond one stock because AI capital expenditure has become large enough to move macro readings, not just tech-sector earnings. A guide this far above consensus signals hyperscaler spending is still accelerating rather than plateauing, which feeds into the same capex and productivity debates the Fed will weigh at Jackson Hole this week. If tonight's number holds up in Thursday's trading, it reinforces the case Warsh can make Friday that growth from AI investment is durable enough to tolerate a slower path on rate cuts — tying a single company's forward guidance directly to how the next FOMC decision gets framed.
